sections.title: AI and Public Policy
sections.description: This course explores the transformative potential of AI in the realm of public policy. Students will delve into the implications of AI for policy practice, learning how to harness AI tools to understand citizen priorities, formulate policy options, and aid decision making processes. Additionally, the course will cover methods for using AI to extract insights from large datasets and academic literature, enabling evidence-based policy development. Co-taught by an AI expert and a policy expert from the University of Pennsylvania, students will gain both a technical grounding in AI tools (including large language models) and a nuanced understanding of policy processes, ethical frameworks, and real-world case studies.

sections.title: AI and Public Policy
sections.description: Governments around the world are already using artificial intelligence: e.g. chatbots that answer residents' questions, tools that support benefit or grant applications, and systems that analyze public comments and administrative data. This course examines how AI is changing the policy-making cycle: the way governments understand problems, design policies, make decisions, implement and evaluate policies. The course is hands-on: using AI coding agents, students build policy-relevant tools and workflows, for example to synthesize research evidence, extract and analyze data from government documents, generate and stress-test policy options, and prototype digital public services. A central emphasis is using AI critically. By combining AI-assisted work with assignments completed without AI, students learn how to use AI in ways that deepen rather than replace their own understanding, and to produce rigorous work that can make a difference in the policy world. The course also addresses the ethical, legal, and regulatory questions raised by AI in the public sector, including bias, accountability, and human oversight. Connecting classroom learning to policy practice, the course typically features guest lectures from policy professionals and assignments designed with input from government or international organizations, such as policy memos written for a public-sector partner.
